09149.explanation: Raw kumquats are recommended during pregnancy as a nutrient-dense citrus fruit. They provide substantial vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber from their edible sweet peels. The FDA advises washing kumquats thoroughly under cool running water before eating them whole. Enjoy them as a fresh snack or sliced thinly into garden salads.

09153.explanation: Commercially bottled lemon juice from concentrate is safe to consume during pregnancy. It supplies vitamin C and acidity to brighten dishes, and commercial bottling ensures pasteurization against foodborne microbes. Use it sparingly if you experience pregnancy heartburn or acid reflux. Splash into water or over cooked fish to add flavor without sodium.

09152.explanation: Freshly squeezed raw lemon juice is safe during pregnancy when prepared with clean handling. It provides vitamin C and potassium, and citrus scents can help ease pregnancy nausea as noted by ACOG. Wash whole lemons under running water before cutting to prevent surface dirt from entering the juice. Squeeze fresh juice into warm water or over roasted vegetables.

09150.explanation: Raw peeled lemons are safe and recommended during pregnancy. They deliver generous amounts of vitamin C that enhance maternal immunity and non-heme iron absorption. The FDA instructs consumers to wash citrus fruit thoroughly before peeling or cutting. Add lemon wedges to herbal teas or ice water to stay hydrated throughout the day.

09161.explanation: Unsweetened bottled lime juice is safe during pregnancy because commercial processing includes pasteurization. It provides vitamin C and tart flavor while remaining free from foodborne bacteria. Be mindful of portion sizes if you are prone to stomach acidity or gastroesophageal reflux. Use a teaspoon to flavor marinades, guacamole, or chilled seltzer.

09160.explanation: Fresh raw lime juice is safe during pregnancy when prepared hygienically at home. It offers vitamin C, potassium, and citric acid, which can stimulate saliva and reduce first-trimester nausea. The FDA recommends washing the entire fruit under running water before slicing with a knife. Squeeze fresh lime over grilled fish or bean dishes to boost plant iron absorption.

09159.explanation: Raw limes are recommended during pregnancy as a nutritious citrus fruit. They provide vitamin C and dietary antioxidants that support connective tissue and collagen formation. Always wash fresh limes under cold running water before cutting to avoid transferring microbes to the flesh. Use fresh lime wedges to brighten roasted poultry and grain bowls.

09165.explanation: Dried litchis are safe during pregnancy when eaten in controlled portions. They supply concentrated vitamin C, riboflavin, and potassium, but drying condenses their natural fruit sugars. Keep serving sizes small to maintain stable blood sugar levels throughout the day. Pair a few dried litchis with a cup of pasteurized cottage cheese for balanced protein.

09164.explanation: Raw fresh litchis are recommended during pregnancy as a hydrating, sweet fruit. They deliver abundant vitamin C, copper, and potassium that support maternal blood volume and immune defense. The FDA suggests washing whole litchis under clean running water before peeling the rough outer shell. Enjoy the juicy white flesh fresh and chilled.

09167.explanation: Frozen loganberries are recommended during pregnancy as a wholesome source of nutrients. They provide vitamin C, folate, and dietary fiber that support fetal neural development and maternal digestion. Frozen fruit maintains peak nutritional value and eliminates the need for chemical preservatives. Thaw gently and mix into morning oatmeal or plain yogurt.

09436.explanation: Canned mango nectar is safe during pregnancy provided it is commercially pasteurized. It offers small amounts of vitamin C, but commercial nectars contain substantial added sweeteners and minimal fiber. The canning process ensures microbial safety against harmful foodborne bacteria. Enjoy an occasional small glass or dilute with chilled seltzer water.

09178.explanation: Sweetened dried mango is safe during pregnancy but requires strict portion moderation. It retains vitamin C and folate, though added refined sugar makes it very high in carbohydrates and calories. Look for unsweetened dried mango strips to reduce unnecessary sugar consumption. Eat a couple of strips alongside walnuts to blunt blood glucose spikes.

09176.explanation: Raw fresh mango is recommended during pregnancy as a nutrient-packed tropical fruit. It supplies folate, vitamin C, and beta-carotene, which support fetal organ development and maternal tissue repair. The FDA advises washing the outer skin under running water before slicing with a clean knife. Cut into cubes and serve alongside grilled chicken or in fresh prenatal smoothies.

09328.explanation: Canned maraschino cherries should be limited during pregnancy. They undergo extensive bleaching and soaking in high-fructose corn syrup and artificial dyes, leaving virtually no natural vitamins. The USDA advises pregnant women to minimize ultra-processed foods with high concentrations of refined sugar. Replace them with fresh sweet cherries or unsweetened frozen cherries.

09181.explanation: Raw cantaloupe is safe and nutritious during pregnancy only when prepared with rigorous hygiene. It provides outstanding amounts of beta-carotene, vitamin C, and potassium that support fetal vision and maternal fluid balance. Because the netted rind can harbor Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella, the FDA and CDC mandate scrubbing the rind with a clean produce brush under running water before cutting. Slice and eat promptly, refrigerating any leftovers immediately below 40°F.

09183.explanation: Raw casaba melon is recommended during pregnancy as a mild, hydrating fruit. It delivers vitamin C, potassium, and vitamin B6 with high water content that assists maternal hydration and kidney filtration. The FDA reminds consumers to wash whole melons thoroughly under running water before slicing. Serve chilled wedges with a sprinkle of lime juice for an afternoon refresher.

09184.explanation: Raw honeydew melon is recommended during pregnancy as an excellent fruit for hydration. It supplies vitamin C, potassium, and B vitamins that aid electrolyte balance and blood pressure regulation. Scrub the outer rind thoroughly with a clean brush under cool running water before slicing to prevent bacterial transfer. Enjoy freshly cubed honeydew as a cool snack or blended into fruit soups.

09190.explanation: Raw mulberries are recommended during pregnancy as an iron-rich fresh berry. They deliver vitamin C, dietary fiber, and plant iron, which help support maternal hemoglobin levels. The FDA and CDC recommend rinsing delicate fresh berries gently in a colander under clean running water just prior to eating. Add fresh mulberries to breakfast cereal or eat them fresh by the handful.

09191.explanation: Raw nectarines are recommended during pregnancy as a nutritious stone fruit. They provide dietary fiber, potassium, and vitamin C that promote healthy digestion and regular bowel movements. The FDA advises washing nectarines thoroughly under clean running water before biting into them or slicing. Enjoy whole fresh nectarines as an easy portable snack on the go.

09195.explanation: Pickled green olives are safe during pregnancy when consumed in moderation. They deliver healthy monounsaturated oleic acid and small amounts of calcium, but the brine carries high sodium levels. Commercial pickling and pasteurization protect against foodborne pathogens. Limit your intake to four or five olives per day to avoid excess sodium retention.

09193.explanation: Canned ripe black olives are safe during pregnancy as an occasional savory addition. They supply plant iron and monounsaturated fats, though canning liquid contributes significant sodium. Commercial canning ensures complete sterility and safety from foodborne illness. Slice a small portion over homemade whole-wheat pizza or Mediterranean salads.

09207.explanation: Canned unsweetened orange juice is safe during pregnancy provided it is pasteurized. It supplies vitamin C, folate, and potassium, but liquid fruit juices lack whole-fruit dietary fiber. The FDA requires commercial canned juices to be heat-treated to destroy harmful bacteria. Drink a single small four-ounce glass alongside a fiber-rich breakfast.

09209.explanation: Chilled pasteurized orange juice is safe to drink during pregnancy in moderate portions. It delivers vitamin C, potassium, and folate, and many commercial brands are fortified with calcium and vitamin D. Commercial pasteurization eliminates dangerous bacterial pathogens like Salmonella. Limit intake to one cup daily to avoid excessive liquid sugar consumption.

09206.explanation: Raw unpasteurized freshly squeezed orange juice presents foodborne illness risks during pregnancy. The FDA and CDC warn that unpasteurized citrus juices can harbor bacterial pathogens such as Salmonella and harmful bacteria. Choose commercially pasteurized orange juice or bring unpasteurized juice to a rolling boil before drinking. If juicing at home, wash the fruit thoroughly and consume immediately.

09200.explanation: Raw whole oranges are highly recommended during pregnancy as an exceptional source of nutrients. They provide folate for fetal spine development, vitamin C for iron absorption, and dietary fiber that prevents constipation. The FDA advises washing whole oranges under running water before peeling so your hands and utensils stay clean. Eat whole fresh orange segments rather than drinking juice to benefit from natural pectin fiber.

09229.explanation: This record contains 57 calories and 3 mg vitamin C per 100 g of canned papaya nectar in PregNut’s historical USDA-based dataset; it describes a food sample, not a suggested serving. FDA advises pregnant people to drink only juice that has been pasteurized or otherwise treated to kill harmful bacteria, and says shelf-stable juice is packaged in treated containers such as boxes, bottles, or cans. The Dietary Guidelines advise avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages such as fruit drinks, so check the nectar label for added sugars.

09226.explanation: Raw papaya is safe during pregnancy only when completely ripe with bright yellow or orange skin. Fully ripe papaya provides beneficial vitamin C, folate, and potassium, whereas unripe green papaya contains concentrated latex and papain that can stimulate uterine contractions. The NHS and ACOG advise pregnant women to strictly avoid unripe or semi-green papaya. Wash ripe papayas under running water before peeling and removing the black seeds.

09232.explanation: Raw unpasteurized purple passion fruit juice carries foodborne safety concerns during pregnancy. The FDA warns that untreated fresh fruit juices can contain harmful bacteria like Salmonella. Consume only commercially pasteurized juices or heat raw juice until it reaches a boil before drinking. Once pasteurized, passion fruit juice provides vitamin C and potassium.

09233.explanation: Raw unpasteurized yellow passion fruit juice is not recommended without proper heat treatment during pregnancy. Untreated juices sold at farm stands or juice bars pose risks of foodborne bacterial infections. The FDA and CDC recommend that expectant mothers choose pasteurized juice products to ensure safety. Check the bottle label to verify pasteurization before purchasing.

09251.explanation: Canned peach nectar is safe during pregnancy when commercially processed. It provides small amounts of vitamin C and potassium, though it is high in refined liquid sugars. Commercial canning heats the product to sterile temperatures, destroying foodborne pathogens. Keep portions moderate and enjoy with a protein snack to steady blood sugar.

09241.explanation: Canned peaches in syrup are safe during pregnancy but should be eaten in moderation. They contain vitamin C and potassium from the fruit, but the heavy syrup adds empty calories and unnecessary sugar. Drain the canning syrup thoroughly or rinse the fruit under water before eating. Mix drained peaches into plain Greek yogurt for extra protein and calcium.

09237.explanation: Canned peaches packed in water are recommended during pregnancy as a convenient fruit option. They supply vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber without the added sugars found in heavy syrup. Sterile canning ensures total safety against foodborne microorganisms. Enjoy canned peaches straight from the bowl or stirred into warm breakfast grains.

09246.explanation: Dried uncooked peaches are recommended during pregnancy as a valuable source of plant iron and potassium. They provide concentrated dietary fiber that helps ease sluggish bowels and prenatal constipation. The USDA recommends drinking plenty of water alongside dried fruit portions. Keep a small bag of dried peaches in your purse for sustained afternoon energy.

09236.explanation: Raw yellow peaches are recommended during pregnancy as a delicious, nutrient-rich stone fruit. They provide dietary fiber, potassium, and vitamin C that help maintain maternal blood pressure and tissue health. The FDA advises washing fresh peaches gently under running water before eating to remove dirt and residues. Slice fresh ripe peaches over morning cereal or eat whole.

09262.explanation: Canned pear nectar is safe during pregnancy as a pasteurized fruit beverage. It provides modest amounts of carbohydrates and hydration, but lacks the natural fiber found in whole pears. Commercial canning ensures microbial sterility and food safety. Limit serving sizes to a small glass to manage overall sugar intake.

09340.explanation: Raw Asian pears are recommended during pregnancy as a refreshing, hydrating fruit. They supply abundant dietary fiber, potassium, and vitamin C, which assist in preventing common prenatal constipation. The FDA advises washing the outer skin thoroughly under running water before slicing with a clean knife. Slice into crisp wedges for an afternoon snack alongside a slice of pasteurized cheese.

09257.explanation: Canned pears in syrup are safe during pregnancy when consumed in moderation. They retain small amounts of dietary fiber and potassium, though sweet syrup adds unnecessary refined sugar. The canning process ensures total protection against foodborne bacterial pathogens. Drain the liquid and rinse the pear halves before serving.

09253.explanation: This record contains 29 calories and 53 mg potassium per 100 g of canned pears in water in PregNut’s historical USDA-based dataset; it describes a food sample, not a suggested serving. CDC says not to eat store-bought canned food if the food or its container shows signs of contamination, and to refrigerate canned foods after opening. The Dietary Guidelines say the sugars naturally present in fruit are not counted as added sugars, so fruit packed in water avoids the added sugar of syrup.

09259.explanation: Dried uncooked pears are recommended during pregnancy as a high-fiber snack. They provide concentrated amounts of potassium, copper, and dietary fiber that support healthy maternal bowel regularity. Drink adequate water when consuming dried fruits to aid fiber digestion. Pair two dried pear halves with pumpkin seeds for a balanced mid-day snack.

09252.explanation: Raw fresh pears are strongly recommended during pregnancy as an exceptional source of dietary fiber. They provide soluble pectin fiber and potassium, which help maintain bowel regularity and stabilize blood sugar. The FDA recommends washing whole pears thoroughly under clean running water before eating with the skin on. Enjoy crisp ripe pears sliced with almond butter.

09263.explanation: Raw Japanese persimmons are recommended during pregnancy when fully ripe. They supply vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber that support immune defense and maternal digestion. The FDA reminds consumers to wash persimmons thoroughly under cold running water before slicing. Eat soft ripe Fuyu persimmons fresh or diced into seasonal salads.

09409.explanation: Unsweetened pineapple juice with added vitamin C is safe during pregnancy when pasteurized. It provides vitamin C and hydration, but lacks the beneficial fiber of whole pineapple and concentrates fruit sugars. The FDA requires commercial shelf-stable juices to be pasteurized to prevent bacterial contamination. Drink a small four-ounce serving with a meal to avoid rapid blood sugar fluctuations.

09270.explanation: This record contains 78 calories, 7.4 mg vitamin C and 104 mg potassium per 100 g of canned pineapple in syrup in PregNut’s historical USDA-based dataset; it describes a food sample, not a suggested serving. NIH’s NCCIH, which covers bromelain as a supplement, says little is known about whether it is safe to use during pregnancy; PregNut has no data on how much bromelain canned pineapple contains. The Dietary Guidelines say no amount of added sugars is recommended and suggest no more than 10 grams per meal; syrup counts as an added sugar, so check the label or drain the syrup.

09266.explanation: Raw fresh pineapple is recommended during pregnancy as a hydrating, vitamin-rich fruit. It supplies substantial vitamin C and folate, and common myths about dietary bromelain causing uterine contractions are unsubstantiated at normal culinary intakes. The FDA instructs consumers to wash the rough outer rind under running water before cutting into the fruit. Enjoy fresh sliced pineapple chilled as a refreshing prenatal snack.

09278.explanation: Cooked plantains are recommended during pregnancy as a nourishing, complex-carbohydrate staple. They provide potassium, vitamin B6, and vitamin C that help sustain maternal energy and support fetal nervous system development. Boiling, baking, or steaming plantains makes their resistant starch easy to digest. Serve cooked savory plantains alongside stewed beans and lean proteins.

09277.explanation: Raw plantains are safe during pregnancy but should generally be cooked prior to consumption. Raw plantains contain dense, ungelatinized starches that can cause bloating, gas, and stomach cramps if eaten uncooked. The USDA recommends cooking plantains by boiling, baking, or roasting until soft. Wash the thick peel under running water before removing it with a knife.

09284.explanation: This record contains 89 calories and 0.84 mg iron per 100 g of canned purple plums in syrup in PregNut’s historical USDA-based dataset; it describes a food sample, not a suggested serving. CDC says not to eat store-bought canned food if the food or its container shows signs of contamination, and to refrigerate canned foods after opening. The Dietary Guidelines say no amount of added sugars is recommended and suggest no more than 10 grams per meal; syrup counts as an added sugar, so check the label or drain the syrup.

09281.explanation: Canned purple plums packed in water are recommended during pregnancy as a wholesome fruit choice. They deliver dietary fiber, potassium, and vitamin C without added refined sugars. The natural sorbitol and fiber in plums gently support digestive transit and help prevent constipation. Enjoy them chilled on their own or mixed into warm oatmeal.

09291.explanation: Dried plums or prunes are strongly recommended during pregnancy as an effective natural remedy for constipation. They provide soluble fiber, potassium, and natural sorbitol, which soften stools and stimulate gentle bowel motility. ACOG and the NHS recommend increasing dietary fiber from foods like prunes to manage prenatal bowel regularity. Eat three to four prunes daily alongside plenty of water.

09279.explanation: Raw fresh plums are recommended during pregnancy as a hydrating, fiber-rich fruit. They supply vitamin C, potassium, and polyphenols that assist tissue growth and vascular health. The FDA and CDC recommend washing plums thoroughly under cold running water before eating. Keep a few ripe plums chilled in the refrigerator for an easy afternoon snack.

09442.explanation: Bottled pomegranate juice is safe to drink during pregnancy when commercially pasteurized. It provides potassium, folate, and polyphenols, but contains concentrated fruit sugars without whole-fruit fiber. The FDA requires commercial shelf-stable bottled juices to undergo pasteurization to protect against foodborne pathogens. Limit your intake to four ounces daily and consider mixing with sparkling water.

09286.explanation: Raw fresh pomegranates are recommended during pregnancy as an antioxidant-rich fruit. The edible seeds provide folate, vitamin C, potassium, and dietary fiber that support fetal development and maternal heart health. The FDA advises washing the outer rind under clean running water before slicing open the fruit to extract the arils. Sprinkle fresh pomegranate seeds over salads, yogurt, or roasted vegetables.

09294.explanation: Canned prune juice is recommended during pregnancy to help relieve sluggish bowels and constipation. It contains sorbitol, potassium, and iron, providing a gentle laxative effect to ease digestive discomfort. Commercial canning provides high-heat pasteurization, ensuring complete safety from harmful microbes. Sip four ounces in the morning alongside a glass of water for digestive regularity.

09297.explanation: Golden seedless raisins are recommended during pregnancy as an iron-rich snack. They supply non-heme iron, potassium, and dietary fiber that help prevent pregnancy anemia and support bowel motility. Check package labels for sulfites if you have known sensitivities to food preservatives. Combine a small handful of golden raisins with walnuts for a balanced snack.

09298.explanation: Seedless raisins are recommended during pregnancy as a convenient, nutrient-dense dried fruit. They provide dietary fiber, potassium, and plant iron to support expanding maternal red blood cell mass. Because dried fruit is calorically dense, measure portions to avoid sudden blood sugar spikes. Toss raisins into warm oatmeal or homemade whole-grain baked goods.

09304.explanation: This record contains 91 calories and 8.7 mg vitamin C per 100 g of canned red raspberries in syrup in PregNut’s historical USDA-based dataset; it describes a food sample, not a suggested serving. CDC says not to eat store-bought canned food if the food or its container shows signs of contamination, and to refrigerate canned foods after opening. The Dietary Guidelines say no amount of added sugars is recommended and suggest no more than 10 grams per meal; syrup counts as an added sugar, so check the label or drain the syrup.

09302.explanation: Raw fresh raspberries are highly recommended during pregnancy as an exceptional source of dietary fiber. They provide vitamin C, folate, and potassium, with eight grams of fiber per cup to support healthy digestion. The FDA and CDC recommend placing raspberries in a sieve and washing them gently under cold running water immediately before eating. Enjoy fresh raspberries on whole-grain waffles or tossed in salads.

09309.explanation: Frozen rhubarb stalks are safe during pregnancy when thoroughly cooked. The tart stalks provide dietary calcium, potassium, and vitamin C, but they must be heated before eating to soften tough fibers. Never consume rhubarb leaves because they contain toxic concentrations of oxalic acid that cause kidney damage. Simmer frozen rhubarb stalks with strawberries and a touch of honey for a safe compote.

09307.explanation: Raw rhubarb stalks are safe during pregnancy once they are washed and cooked. The edible stalks deliver calcium, vitamin C, and fiber, but the broad green leaves are highly toxic due to severe oxalic acid content and must always be discarded. Wash the stalks thoroughly under clean running water before trimming. Bake or stew rhubarb stalks with sweet fruits like apples or berries to balance tartness.

09315.explanation: Raw soursop is safe to consume in small, occasional culinary amounts during pregnancy. It supplies vitamin C and potassium, but pregnant women must avoid concentrated medicinal extracts or teas made from soursop leaves due to neurotoxic annonacin compounds. The FDA advises washing whole tropical fruits under clean running water before slicing. Eat modest portions of the fresh ripe fruit pulp while discarding the toxic seeds.

09317.explanation: Canned strawberries in syrup are safe during pregnancy when eaten in moderation. They supply vitamin C and folate, but the packing syrup contributes high levels of refined sugar. Commercial canning provides sterile packaging, ensuring safety from bacterial contamination. Drain and rinse the fruit pieces before adding them to pancakes or desserts.

09316.explanation: Raw fresh strawberries are highly recommended during pregnancy as an outstanding source of vitamin C and folate. They deliver antioxidants, potassium, and dietary fiber that support fetal neural development and maternal blood vessel health. The FDA and CDC recommend washing strawberries thoroughly under cold running water right before removing their green caps to prevent waterlogging and contamination. Enjoy fresh sliced strawberries over whole-grain cereal or in yogurt bowls.

09322.explanation: Raw tamarind pulp is safe during pregnancy when used in normal culinary quantities. It supplies non-heme iron, magnesium, and potassium, which help support red blood cell production and muscle relaxation. Avoid large medicinal doses or concentrated extracts because concentrated tamarind has mild laxative properties. Use a small amount of paste to flavor savory curries or lentil stews.
